actions.title: ZOAM-2024-0001 / CPAM-2024-0001 — Data Center Standards & Locations, Phase 1

scope_decode.summary: Not a prohibition. Eliminates by-right (administrative) approval of data centers in the Industrial Park (IP), General Industry (GI), and Mineral Resources-Heavy Industry (MR-HI) districts; new data center uses now require Special Exception (SPEX) approval, a legislative review with public hearings before both the Planning Commission and the Board of Supervisors. Companion CPAM-2024-0001 designates data centers a conditional use in the 2019 General Plan.

pending_application_carveout.note: Yes, but narrow. The Board adopted a companion Grandfathering Resolution: data center applications accepted for review before February 12, 2025 may continue processing without SPEX approval — but, per the County's published summary and Holland & Knight's analysis, only for proposed data centers located more than 500 feet from residential areas, and only absent substantial changes to the application. Pending applications closer to residential areas lost their by-right path.

actions.vesting_context: Virginia: Va. Code § 15.2-2307. Vesting requires a significant affirmative governmental act (e.g., approved rezoning, special exception, or site plan) plus good-faith reliance and substantial expense. A pending application, standing alone, generally does NOT vest rights in Virginia — which is why Loudoun's grandfathering resolution, not the vesting statute, is doing the work for in-process projects.
actions.numeric_standards: SPEX now required for data center use in IP, GI and MR-HI districts. Grandfathering limited to applications accepted before Feb. 12, 2025 on sites more than 500 ft from residential areas. Phase 2 (performance standards — noise, design, siting criteria) in development as of 2026.
actions.entitlement_path: Formerly by-right in key industrial districts; now special exception (SPEX) county-wide for new applications. Loudoun uses 'special exception,' not CUP, terminology.
actions.editorial_analysis: Editorial analysis: The world's largest data center market just converted its core product — fast administrative approval — into a discretionary legislative process. Expect SPEX timelines of 12-18+ months, proffer-style negotiation pressure, and a repricing of land that was bought at by-right values. The 500-foot grandfathering line is the immediate battleground: pending applications near residential edges lost their lane on adoption day. Phase 2 performance standards are the next event to watch.

actions.title: PW Digital Gateway rezonings — voided ab initio by circuit court

scope_decode.summary: Status shown as 'repealed' for filtering purposes; the precise posture is judicial invalidation, not legislative repeal. On Aug. 7, 2025 the Prince William Circuit Court (Judge Kimberly Irving) declared the rezoning ordinances for the ~2,100-acre Digital Gateway corridor (approved after the Dec. 12, 2023 public hearing) void ab initio for failure to comply with Va. Code § 15.2-2204 public-notice requirements — notice published only days before the hearing, without the rezoning documents available for review.

pending_application_carveout.note: Not applicable — this is litigation over an approval, not a restriction with a carve-out. The relevant lesson runs the other way: an approval void ab initio is treated as if it never existed, so nothing downstream of it (site plans, permits) can support vesting.

actions.vesting_context: Virginia: Va. Code § 15.2-2307 requires a significant affirmative governmental act plus good-faith reliance. A rezoning declared void ab initio is legally no act at all — meaning reliance expenditures on the Digital Gateway approvals likely cannot generate vested rights. Procedural compliance diligence (notice, advertisement, document availability) is therefore a title-grade issue for data center M&A in Virginia.
actions.numeric_standards: Project as approved: ~2,100-acre corridor along Pageland Lane near Gainesville; reported at over 22 million sq ft across up to 37 data center buildings at full buildout.
actions.entitlement_path: Rezoning-based (legislative). After invalidation, the land reverts to its prior zoning; any new attempt requires a fresh rezoning with compliant notice.
actions.litigation: Oak Valley homeowners' challenge. Aug. 7, 2025: circuit court voids rezonings ab initio (Va. Code § 15.2-2204 notice defects). Nov. 2025: construction barred pending appeal. The Virginia Court of Appeals upheld the circuit court; in April 2026, Compass Datacenters dropped its appeal, leaving the invalidation in place.
actions.editorial_analysis: Editorial analysis: The largest planned data center campus in the world was undone not on the merits but on a notice defect — three days of notice instead of the statutory minimum, with documents unavailable. That is now the template for opposition groups statewide: procedural attack is cheaper than substantive attack and, as here, fully dispositive. Buyers of entitled Virginia land should treat hearing-notice compliance files as diligence documents on par with the proffers themselves.

actions.title: Data Center Zoning Ordinance Amendment (effective Sept. 11, 2024)

scope_decode.summary: Not a prohibition. Adds detailed use standards for data centers and caps by-right size; projects that exceed the by-right thresholds or cannot meet the standards require Special Exception approval (except in the I-5 and I-6 districts). In practice, most new data centers in Fairfax now route through Special Exception.

pending_application_carveout.note: The amendment took effect Sept. 11, 2024, the day after adoption. Specific transition language for applications pending on the effective date has not yet been verified against the adopted ordinance text — verify before relying.

actions.vesting_context: Virginia: Va. Code § 15.2-2307. A pending application generally does not vest; a project with an approved site plan or special exception before the effective date stands on much stronger ground. Fairfax uses 'special exception' terminology.
actions.numeric_standards: By-right size caps: 40,000 sq ft in C-3 and C-4 (retained); 80,000 sq ft in I-2, I-3 and I-4 (new). Larger projects require Special Exception except in I-5/I-6. Data center buildings: minimum 200 ft from the lot line of adjacent residential districts/uses. The 200/300-foot residential setbacks are now a de facto regional floor; expect them cited in every Northern Virginia ordinance fight. For site selection, I-5 and I-6 parcels carry a measurable entitlement premium.

actions.vesting_context: Georgia: common-law vesting. Rights generally vest on issuance of a building permit, or on substantial expenditures made in good-faith reliance on existing zoning or on the probability of permit issuance. A pre-ordinance land closing alone is weak; a pre-ordinance building permit is strong.

For developers this is actually the easy case: the rule is clear, the excluded zone is mappable, and the rest of the metro remains open. The harder Georgia risk now sits in the suburban counties (see DeKalb, Coweta, Douglas, Cobb entries), where the rules are still moving.

actions.title: One-year data center moratorium — rescinded after federal lawsuit; review checklist adopted

scope_decode.summary: Adopted May 12, 2026 (3-2, commissioners court) as a moratorium of up to one year on data center development in rural Hill County — reportedly the first Texas county to attempt one. Replaced the same day with a development review checklist requiring information on water use, traffic, noise and economic effects, plus expanded public-notice requirements (notice to nearby residents and local media for major projects).

pending_application_carveout.note: Moot after rescission. actions.vesting_context: Texas: Loc. Gov't Code ch. 245 — permit rights vest at the filing of the first permit application in a series, freezing the regulations applicable to the project. Separately, Texas counties (unlike home-rule cities) hold only powers expressly granted or necessarily implied by statute, and have no general zoning authority — the threshold defect RCM Hill's federal suit targeted here.

Replacement checklist: disclosure of expected water use, traffic impacts, noise levels, economic effects; notice to nearby residents and local media for major projects. actions.litigation: RCM Hill, LLC v. Hill County (federal): filed late May 2026, alleging the county exceeded its statutory authority; per KERA and Texas Tribune reporting, the suit remained active even after the moratorium was rescinded.
actions.editorial_analysis: Editorial analysis: The fastest collapse of a data center moratorium on record, and the clearest demonstration that the Texas county toolkit is fundamentally different from Virginia's or Georgia's: no zoning power, ch. 245 vesting on first filing, and a developer bar ready to litigate. Expect opposition energy in Texas to flow toward cities (which do have zoning — see Harlingen, Fort Worth) and toward the Legislature, not county courthouses. The surviving lawsuit may yet produce a published opinion that settles county authority statewide.

E) imposes procedural requirements (public hearings, findings) that Harlingen visibly followed — and ch. 245 independently protects projects whose first permit application predates the pause.

actions.vesting_context: Texas: Loc. Gov't Code ch. 245 — rights vest at filing of the first permit application in a series, locking in then-current regulations for the project. A data center prospect that filed anything in the permit chain before May 20, 2026 has a strong statutory argument that the moratorium and any later-adopted standards cannot be applied to it.
actions.numeric_standards: 120-day term from adoption (expiry date not stated in cited reporting; verify against ordinance text). Two public hearings held before adoption.
actions.entitlement_path: City zoning applies (unlike Texas counties). New data center applications paused; the city has signaled new land-use regulations for data centers as the end product.
actions.editorial_analysis: Editorial analysis: Harlingen is the careful counter-example to Hill County — a city with actual zoning power, following the ch. 212 moratorium procedure step by step (initiation vote, dual hearings, findings) before adopting. That procedural discipline makes this pause far more defensible, and it previews the playbook other Texas cities will copy as hyperscale interest moves into secondary markets like the Rio Grande Valley. The ch. 245 first-filing question is still the whole game for the two prospects already circling.

actions.title: Proposed data center regulations — zoning, noise, water, incentives package

scope_decode.summary: Proposed standards, not a pause. City staff unveiled a regulatory package (reported early June 2026) covering zoning, noise standards, water utility requirements and economic development incentives. Key proposals: mandatory closed-loop cooling for all new data centers; standby generator testing limited to weekdays 8 a.m.-5 p.m. (with TCEQ-regulated and emergency exceptions); prohibition of cryptocurrency mining as a primary use. Residents had separately pushed for a full moratorium, which the city has not adopted; the council has not yet voted on the package.

pending_application_carveout.note: Not yet drafted/published. Under Texas Loc. Gov't Code ch. 245, projects with a first permit application on file before any new ordinance takes effect would generally be exempt from the new standards regardless of what transition language says — the statute is the carve-out.

actions.vesting_context: Texas: Loc. Gov't Code ch. 245 — first-application vesting freezes applicable regulations project-wide. With four data center developments (10 buildings, 3M+ sq ft) already in the city and more in the pipeline, the practical reach of the new rules will be limited to projects that have not yet started their permit series when the ordinance passes — an incentive to file now.
actions.numeric_standards: As proposed: closed-loop cooling required for all new data centers; generator testing weekdays 8 a.m.-5 p.m. only (emergency/TCEQ exceptions); cryptocurrency mining prohibited as primary use. Specific dBA limits and setbacks not yet published.
actions.entitlement_path: Fort Worth's current code does not specifically define or regulate data centers; projects proceed under general industrial zoning (an April 2026 zoning commission approval advanced a major project under existing rules). The package would create a defined use with tailored standards.
actions.editorial_analysis: Editorial analysis: Fort Worth is writing rules for a market that already exists inside its limits — which, combined with ch. 245, means the ordinance will mostly govern the next generation of projects, not the current one. The closed-loop cooling mandate is the consequential piece: it converts the water fight into an engineering spec and may become the model provision for water-stressed Texas cities. Watch for the filing surge between publication of the draft and the council vote.

actions.title: 150-day data center moratorium — pending application expressly NOT exempted; extended Nov. 2025

scope_decode.summary: Active, and unusually broad. Adopted July 1, 2025 (4-2, Fiscal Court): 150-day pause on any application to build a data center. Critically, the court struck draft language that would have exempted the already-filed Western Hospitality Partners application ('Project Lincoln,' a proposed ~$6B, 600 MW campus on 267 acres, with a 100 MW first phase) — deliberately sweeping a pending application into the pause. On Nov. 18, 2025 the Fiscal Court approved a further moratorium extending the pause until data center regulations are adopted (no fixed end date).

pending_application_carveout.note: Affirmatively refused. Most moratoria exempt complete applications already on file; Oldham's Fiscal Court struck that exact exemption from the draft, capturing WHP's pending Project Lincoln application. WHP subsequently dropped the project after sustained public backlash (per WDRB). This is the cleanest recent example of a pending application providing no protection absent a vesting statute.

actions.vesting_context: Kentucky: no ch. 245-style statute; vesting follows common-law principles generally requiring permit issuance plus substantial reliance. Kentucky is outside Vested's primer states (TX/VA/GA) — treat this note as orientation, and verify Kentucky doctrine with counsel before relying.
actions.numeric_standards: Initial term: 150 days (July 1 - late Nov. 2025). Nov. 18, 2025 extension: open-ended until regulations are adopted. Captured project: reported 600 MW / $6B across 267 acres (100 MW initial application).
actions.entitlement_path: All data center applications paused county-wide until the Fiscal Court adopts data center regulations.
actions.editorial_analysis: Editorial analysis: Oldham is the cautionary tale for the 'we filed, we're safe' assumption: the Fiscal Court struck the pending-application exemption on the record, the captured project died, and the moratorium then went open-ended. June 2026 primary elections in Kentucky were fought partly on data center politics, so the regulatory end-state remains genuinely uncertain. In states without statutory vesting, the carve-out clause — not the filing date — is the entire risk analysis.
